figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. The diversity and biosynthesis of taxanes.
The central circle illustrates the MEP and MVA pathways, which catalyze the formation of GGPP. The upper section represents the MEP pathway,
synthesizing GGPP from pyruvate, whereas the lower section depicts the MVA pathway, synthesizing GGPP from acetyl-CoA. The first ring displays the
11 known taxane skeletons, from types I to XI. The second ring shows potential intermediates involved in the synthesis of representative compounds. The
third (outermost) ring presents representative compounds derived from the corresponding skeletons. In the color bar, blue indicates taxane skeletons
with known and well-defined metabolic pathways, such as the biosynthesis of paclitaxel; white indicates unknown taxane biosynthetic pathways.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Different modules used to construct the taxane library.
(A) The TXS open conformation, complexed with three clustered Mg2+ ions and the ligand GGPP, is shown in green. The TXS closed conformation,
complexed with Mg2+ ions and the ligand GGPP and predicted by AlphaFold 3, is shown in sky blue. Three loops functioning as lids are colored salmon
(D80–S93), lemon (S569–R580), and magenta (Y835–E846), respectively.
(B) Left: the structure of taxadiene, with orange-labeled carbon atoms representing the intrinsic chiral centers of the skeleton and blue-labeled carbon
atoms indicating new chiral centers formed after substitution. Center: seven distinct reported modifications of taxadiene; light green indicates regions
catalyzed by CYP450s, and light yellow indicates regions catalyzed by the BAHD protein family. Right: a comparison of the actual number of taxadiene-
derived compounds with the theoretical number of compounds generated by various combinations of modification types.
(C) A comprehensive collection of modification types currently observed in taxane compounds. Modifications catalyzed by CYP450s are shown in light
green, whereas those catalyzed by the BAHD protein family are shown in light yellow.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Synthetic biology strategies supporting taxane biosynthesis.
(A) Gene identification in the taxane biosynthetic pathway. This process includes sequential steps such as omics data mining, phylogenetic analysis,
metabolic network analysis, and the assembly of heterologous biosynthetic pathways.
(B) Regulatory strategies for taxane biosynthesis. On the left side of the dashed line is the compartmentalization strategy. The first row depicts organelles,
including the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus; the second row shows the chloroplast and mitochondrion. The right side of the dashed line
presents synthetic biology regulatory toolkits based on the CRISPRi-dCas9 reversible gene circuit platform. This includes CRISPRi-dCas9-based NOR
gate circuits and combinations of promoters and enhancers of varying strengths.
(C) Metabolon engineering strategies for taxane biosynthesis. During substrate channeling, enzymes A, B, and C enable rapid transfer of substrates and
intermediates, ensuring efficient synthesis of the target product E. In the absence of substrate channeling, enzyme A may compete with enzyme D for
substrate I, leading to the formation of the non-target byproduct F. This byproduct may introduce toxic interference in the pathway, considerably im-
pairing the efficiency and yield of the desired product.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Deep learning integrates natural product prediction and protein evolution to accelerate molecular design.
(A) A deep-learning-based framework for natural product prediction. The process involves obtaining biosynthetic pathway and molecular structure data
from databases (e.g., KEGG, Reactome, MetaCyc); using SMILES to represent molecular structures; utilizing graph neural networks to extract molecular
topological features; combining these features with Transformer encoders to learn molecular sequences and contextual information; and finally, pre-
dicting possible molecular structures of natural products, annotating key functional groups (in red) and pathway information, and guiding the synthesis
and optimization of natural products.
(B) AI-based directed evolution of proteins. A variant library is generated through gene diversification; variants are amplified, expressed, and screened;
and mutation data are integrated with artificial intelligence models to predict protein performance and function. The AI model uses the relationship
between screening results and sequence information to guide the next round of mutation design, enabling rapid, directional optimization of protein
performance and accelerating the process of protein engineering.
